title: What I learned from building a $18 AI-assisted, Three-Body-inspired visual novel
author: Working-Row-7129
selftext: I recently finished a small visual novel prototype inspired by the three-body problem.This isn’t an adaptation of the novels or TV series, and I didn’t use any official assets. My goal was to explore a more general idea: can a short, choice-driven game make the player feel small in a universe governed by forces they don’t fully understand?I also wanted to test how far I could take the prototype with a very limited AI budget.My workflow was fairly simple. I started with a short narrative outline and reduced it to a small number of playable scenes. Instead of trying to generate the whole game at once, I worked scene by scene: build one interaction, play it, identify the most obvious problem, and then revise it.The difficult part wasn’t generating more content. It was maintaining continuity between scenes and deciding what to remove. Whenever I changed the pacing or structure of one scene, I had to check whether the surrounding dialogue, visuals, and transitions still made sense.Sound also became much more important than I expected.Some scenes initially felt like static images with text. Adding a larger, more cinematic soundscape gave them a much stronger sense of scale—but it also created a new problem. If the audio became too dramatic, it competed with the writing instead of supporting it. I ended up testing the same scenes repeatedly with different audio levels and timing.I used Seele AI to create and iterate on the playable prototype. It wasn’t a one-prompt result: the process involved multiple rounds of generation, playtesting, editing, and removing things that didn’t work.The prototype consumed approximately $18 in AI credits. That number does not include my own time, existing hardware, internet access, or tools I already owned. It represents the direct AI cost of reaching the current playable prototype, not the complete cost of developing and shipping a commercial game.My main takeaway is that AI made it much faster to reach something playable, but it didn’t solve the design decisions. I still had to determine whether a scene was understandable, whether a choice felt meaningful, and whether the audiovisual presentation improved the story or simply made it louder.I’ve attached a short, unedited gameplay clip along with a few screenshots from different stages of development.I’d particularly appreciate feedback on two questions:Does the sound design add a sense of scale, or does it distract from the text?Does the slower pacing create tension, or does it make the interaction feel passive?I’m also curious how other developers evaluate AI-assisted narrative prototypes. What do you test first: the writing, the choices, or the overall atmosphere?
